card.story_form: second-person historical fiction: one invented soldier's whole war, from draft letter to old age, carried by keepsakes and a promise
card.editorial_summary: [I] Under the D-Day set piece, the video is about what a war takes from an ordinary man and what he carries home: a photograph from his girlfriend, a dead friend's silver case, and one carved word ('Move'). Each object is planted early, changes meaning as people die, and returns at the end, when the old man finally sets the case down on the beach and walks away from the water by choice. Invented characters (Ruth, Eddie, Miller, Billy) inside real events (Omaha Beach, the hedgerows, Saint-Lo, the surrender).
card.title_promise: [O] title 'POV: You Are a Soldier in World War 2'; thumbnail: [O] seen (a big-eyed young soldier in the cartoon style). [I] Promises immersion: the war lived from inside one man's boots rather than explained.
card.visual_medium: detailed cartoon stills (big-eyed round faces, warm painted backgrounds) with no camera motion, comic-panel splits and thought-bubble insets, small place-and-date caption boxes
card.narrator_character: [I] An intimate storyteller who speaks to 'you' in the present tense, like a voice inside your own memory: plain words, short declaratives, emotional understatement ('Ruth does not. Not at first.'), aphorisms that grow from scenes ('Fear with no release has nowhere to go', 'Courage does not look like the posters'), and dialogue reported in a few words. No jokes except the characters' own (Eddie's 'amazing how bullets respect arrows').

card.story_form: second-person 'one day in the life' reconstruction, clocked hour by hour, that corrects the movie picture of war
card.editorial_summary: [I] The video argues that an infantryman's war was mostly work and waiting that made the rare fighting possible and frightening. It follows one representative rifleman through one July day in Normandy, hour by hour, turning every chore (digging, rations, latrines, feet, water, ammunition, patrol, mail, watch) into a small lesson with a payoff, plants a 'most dangerous sentence' early and pays it off at night, and closes on a receipt of the day: zero rounds fired, every hour spent being ready.
card.title_promise: [O] title 'What Did WW2 Soldiers Actually Do All Day'; thumbnail: a smiling soldier dozing under an apple tree with a rifle across his lap, men digging and reading behind him, smoke on the horizon, caption 'NO FIGHTING'. [I] Promises a myth-busting, surprisingly ordinary answer; 'NO FIGHTING' overstates it, since the video includes a mortar strike and a night alarm.
card.visual_medium: painted-cartoon stills (round white faces, soft painted backgrounds) with slow pans and zooms, burned-in word-highlight captions at the bottom, flat infographic cards on graph paper, clock title cards, top-down maps, labels and stamps
card.narrator_character: [I] A wry, warm companion speaking to 'you' throughout: dry one-line jokes ('stop having elbows', 'enemy machinery' for a snorer, 'nearly ends both of your careers through embarrassment'), plain explanation, frequent myth-versus-reality asides ('That's the part war movies usually skip'), and honest uncertainty ('I don't know. That is the most common honest answer in war'). Never mocks the soldiers; humour comes from their situation.

hook.promise: What did a soldier actually do all day? Not what the movies show; and a warning that the night's 'everything is quiet' will be the most dangerous sentence of the day.
